conversation.title: What's shaping your vote on the immigration questions?

comments.author: Erin Obourn
comments.text: Welcome Rukhsar, a multiplatform reporter with CBC Calgary:

comments.author: Rukhsar Ali
comments.text:
For some Albertans, this is personal — family members, co-workers or neighbours whose future here depends on how these rules land. For others, it's about how the province grows and changes — housing, jobs, services — and what that means long-term. Often, it's a mix of both.

So let’s talk about the policy side of things, with respect for the people it affects. What aspect of this matters most to you and why? ~ Rukhsar Ali, CBC

(Comments are moderated for civility. Comments flagged for the moderator after 8 p.m. MT will be processed the following day.)

comments.author: Johannes Dietz
comments.text:
It is really striking that this question, like many others, is designed to split people. Into us and them.
There is no evidence of voter fraud. It is not an issue. But it is being made one by this campaign, with no other purpose that introducing division.
That should be disturbing to every Canadian.

comments.author: seuno
comments.text: I am a temporary resident living and working with Alberta under the Canada-Ukraine Authorization for Emergency Travel (CUAET) program. I've been paying taxes since the first day of arriving in Canada, long before I became a tax resident which is 18 months post-arrival to Canada. While I cannot vote on this referendum, some of the issues it raises affects me and I have some issues with some of the underlying assumptions. Take for instance the question of charging non 'Alberta-approved' temporary residents for healthcare for instance because they're not 'contributing' to the economy. Since there is currently no such immigration status as 'Alberta-approved temporary resident', it's safe to assume that every Ukrainian and their families living and working in Alberta under the CUAET program are temporary residents. So much so because the cited 246,000 temporary residents living in Alberta includes CUAET holders, and likely constitute a majority of that number. So the assumption of 'let's charge the temporary residents' because 'they're not contributing to the economy, why should they get any benefits' is problematic and not based on facts. And let's not talk about the Alberta is calling campaign. The province is citing immigration as the cause of strain on its infrastructure and resources, and likely so, but refuses to mention the impact that its own campaign inviting people to come from other parts of Canada (which likely includes both citizens, PRs, and temporary residents) has played in putting pressure on public resources. I cannot vote on this, unfortunately, but I can say that the referendum, including both the questions asked and how they're being asked, are not in good faith and its doing a disservice to the people who are working and contributing to Alberta while being painted as a pest or a parasite on the province's resources rather than positive contributors.

comments.author: Chris Blando
comments.text: This proposed decision clearly demonstrates that the UCP government is completely out of touch with the hospitality/tourist industry. Many hotels and restaurants rely heavily on temporary foreign workers. As noted by Nenshi, these people already pay their fair share of taxes. Many of the jobs these workers are employed to perform occur during times when Alberta’s youth are back in school. So who do they hire to perform these duties during the school months? I would suggest these business have tried their best to hire Albertans, but for various reasons their efforts have fallen short. I would further argue that the UCP refuses to provide actual numbers because the problems that the Alberta healthcare system is currently experiencing is the results of mismanagement. They are simply trying to dump the greater problem on a small group of individuals. I think it would help all Albertans understand the problem if the UCP government were to provide verifiable information detailing the tax revenue versus the healthcare costs associated temporary foreign workers. This might alleviate the perception that the UCP government’s proposed policies are driven more from a racist point of view.

comments.author: Anil Singh
comments.text:
Ms. Ali
​I have been a proud resident of Alberta since 2008, when I first arrived as a Temporary Foreign Worker from Mumbai. My journey to build a life here in Canada has been one of immense dedication and hard work. When I faced a setback in 2010 because I did not meet the high school educational requirements for the Alberta Immigrant Nominee Program (AINP), I challenged myself to earn my Canadian GED. For 90 days, I worked full-time as a housekeeper and studied relentlessly, often surviving on just three hours of sleep a night. I pushed forward and continued to upskill, eventually earning my Class 5 Power Engineering certification and my CDCTP from the Uptime Institute.
​Because I was so deeply focused on surviving and securing a stable foundation for my family, I unfortunately misunderstood the strict age limits surrounding family sponsorship. While I was incredibly grateful to finally bring my wife, Reeta, and my youngest son, Harsh, to Canada, we were devastated to learn that my eldest son, Indrajit, was excluded from the application simply because he had passed the 22-year age cutoff.
​Today, there is an empty chair at our dining table every single night. Reeta, Harsh, and I are active, tax-paying members of our community, and we proudly volunteer our time at a local cancer hospital. Meanwhile, Indrajit remains separated from us in India. He is highly qualified, holding a Master’s degree in Cybersecurity and a Certified Ethical Hacker designation. He has received multiple calls from Alberta companies eager to hire him, but the moment they realize he is overseas, they back away, expressing fear that the government will reject or complicate the sponsorship paperwork.
​Canada beautifully champions the value of family reunification—allowing parents to arrive on Super Visas and making exceptions to sponsor dependents over 22 who have physical or mental disabilities. I respectfully ask: why isn't there a more accessible pathway for highly qualified adult children whose entire immediate family is already established and contributing to Canada? Indrajit is ready to bring his in-demand tech skills to Alberta, pay taxes, and help grow the economy.
​I know this is a complex system, but I want my voice to be heard on behalf of families like mine who are split apart by this policy. I sincerely hope that the government will consider creating pathways that allow families to finally be whole again.
Please bring this to the government attention that they should keep atleast family sponsorship on table, or increase the age of kids to 30 years old.
